title: Command-line bioinformatics and reproducible execution
text:
Biological question and data
Can the same file-processing task run independently of an interactive R session?
This portable exercise launches the Rscript executable belonging to the current R installation. It requires no Unix shell or external bioinformatics program. It illustrates the command-line interface pattern used by larger tools.
No biological download is required. Numerical inputs are hypothetical, not observed animal data. The runnable examples use base R. Count and abundance units are specified where used.

title: Command-line bioinformatics and reproducible execution
section: 1. Create a small input and worker script
text:
1. Create a small input and worker script
Both files live in a fresh temporary directory. The script takes exactly one input argument and validates it.


Show R code
work <- tempfile("cli-example-"); dir.create(work)
input <- file.path(work,"sample counts.csv")
write.csv(data.frame(sample=c("s1","s2","s3"),count=c(10,20,30)),input,row.names=FALSE)
worker <- file.path(work,"summarise.R")
writeLines(c('args <- commandArgs(trailingOnly=TRUE)',
 'stopifnot(length(args)==1L, file.exists(args[1]))',
 'd <- read.csv(args[1])',
 'stopifnot(all(c("sample","count") %in% names(d)))',
 'cat(sum(d$count), "\n")'),worker)
readLines(worker)


[1] "args <- commandArgs(trailingOnly=TRUE)"               
[2] "stopifnot(length(args)==1L, file.exists(args[1]))"    
[3] "d <- read.csv(args[1])"                               
[4] "stopifnot(all(c(\"sample\",\"count\") %in% names(d)))"
[5] "cat(sum(d$count), \""                                 
[6] "\")"                                                  


Explicit arguments make the worker independent of objects in the current global environment.

title: Command-line bioinformatics and reproducible execution
text:
2. Run and capture the process
Quote each path as a separate argument, including the intentionally spaced input filename.


Show R code
executable <- file.path(R.home("bin"),if(.Platform$OS.type=="windows") "Rscript.exe" else "Rscript")
output <- system2(executable,args=c("--vanilla",shQuote(worker),shQuote(input)),
 stdout=TRUE,stderr=TRUE)
status <- attr(output,"status"); if(is.null(status)) status <- 0L
c(status=status,total=as.numeric(tail(output,1)))


status  total 
     0     60 


Show R code
stopifnot(status==0L,as.numeric(tail(output,1))==60)


The worker reports 60 and exits successfully. Locale-startup messages may appear before the final number on some systems.

title: Command-line bioinformatics and reproducible execution
text:
3. Describe the workflow boundary
Record executable, arguments, input and expected output before applying this pattern to another tool.


Show R code
record <- data.frame(step="sum counts",executable=basename(executable),
 input=basename(input),output="stdout total",expected_total=60)
record


        step  executable             input       output expected_total
1 sum counts Rscript.exe sample counts.csv stdout total             60


For a real aligner, include reference, version, options, resource requirements and the meaning of each output. A zero exit code does not certify biological correctness.

title: Command-line bioinformatics and reproducible execution
text:
Interpretation and limits
Use tool-specific documentation for real aligners or quantifiers; this example runs no alignment. Keep restricted data out of command logs and public repositories. Temporary files are left in R’s temporary directory for inspection.

What changes if the worker relies on an interactive variable?
Why quote the filename?
Which check remains necessary after a successful exit?

A clean Rscript process does not contain that variable.
Spaces must stay within one argument.
Check output structure, sample/reference identity and scientific plausibility, not just process completion.

title: Alignment and conserved-region analysis
text:
Biological question and data
How do alignment and missingness decisions change the apparent conservation of a region?
The local helper uses Needleman–Wunsch global alignment with fixed match, mismatch and linear-gap scores. The multiple alignment is supplied, not inferred by this pairwise helper.
No biological download is required. Numerical inputs are hypothetical, not observed animal data. The runnable examples use base R. Count and abundance units are specified where used.

title: Alignment and conserved-region analysis
section: 1. Align two sequences under stated scores
text:
1. Align two sequences under stated scores
Global alignment compares the entire supplied sequences. Different scoring choices can change an optimal alignment.


Show R code
source("../R/sequence_helpers.R")
a <- "ACGTACGT"; b <- "ACGACGT"
fit <- global_alignment(a,b)
fit


$a
[1] "ACGTACGT"

$b
[1] "ACG-ACGT"

$score
[1] 12


Show R code
stopifnot(gsub("-","",fit$a)==a,gsub("-","",fit$b)==b,
 nchar(fit$a)==nchar(fit$b),fit$score==12)
self <- global_alignment(a,a)
stopifnot(self$score==2*nchar(a),self$a==a,self$b==a)


Seven matches and one gap produce a score of 12 under +2/−1/−2 scoring. The score is not an evolutionary distance.

title: Alignment and conserved-region analysis
text:
2. Inspect an existing multiple alignment
A column is conservatively called conserved only when every sequence supplies a nucleotide and all those nucleotides match.


Show R code
aligned <- c(s1="ACGTACGT",s2="ACG-ACGT",s3="ACGTTCGN")
M <- do.call(rbind,strsplit(aligned,""))
called <- M%in%c("A","C","G","T"); dim(called) <- dim(M)
fully_called <- colSums(called)==nrow(M)
conserved <- apply(M,2,function(z) all(z%in%c("A","C","G","T")) && length(unique(z))==1)
data.frame(position=seq_len(ncol(M)),fully_called,conserved)


  position fully_called conserved
1        1         TRUE      TRUE
2        2         TRUE      TRUE
3        3         TRUE      TRUE
4        4        FALSE     FALSE
5        5         TRUE     FALSE
6        6         TRUE      TRUE
7        7         TRUE      TRUE
8        8        FALSE     FALSE


Show R code
stopifnot(sum(fully_called)==6,sum(conserved)==5)


A gap and an unknown base are excluded from fully called columns; a genuine nucleotide difference breaks conservation in another column.

title: Alignment and conserved-region analysis
text:
3. Compare denominators
Calculate both the fraction of all alignment columns and the fraction of fully called columns that are conserved.


Show R code
c(conserved_of_all=sum(conserved)/ncol(M),
 conserved_of_fully_called=sum(conserved)/sum(fully_called))


         conserved_of_all conserved_of_fully_called 
                0.6250000                 0.8333333 


These fractions answer different questions. Report the denominator and missingness rather than choosing the larger value.

title: Alignment and conserved-region analysis
text:
Interpretation and limits
The example does not identify an actual functional element. Conservation depends on alignment quality, phylogenetic diversity and evolutionary processes. Production multiple aligners and evolutionary conservation models need their own method choices and diagnostics.

Change the gap score and inspect the result.
Why is N not evidence for a conserved base?
Why does conservation alone not prove function?







Suggested answers






Alternative alignments can become optimal, particularly where mismatch and gap alternatives compete.
Its nucleotide is unknown.
Context, species sampling, evolutionary constraints and biological evidence determine the interpretation.

title: Protein structure and structural bioinformatics
text:
Biological question and data
Which residue pairs lie close together in a supplied protein-coordinate model?
The six coordinates are invented C-alpha positions in angstroms, not a protein database structure. Euclidean proximity is calculated under a supplied cutoff; consecutive residues are excluded from the contact summary.
No biological download is required. Numerical inputs are hypothetical, not observed animal data. The runnable examples use base R. Count and abundance units are specified where used.

title: Protein structure and structural bioinformatics
text:
1. Inspect coordinates and distances
Rows represent residues. Distance is calculated in the stated coordinate system.


Show R code
xyz <- rbind(c(0,0,0),c(3.8,0,0),c(7.6,0,0),c(7.6,3.8,0),c(3.8,3.8,0),c(0,3.8,0))
rownames(xyz) <- paste0("residue",1:6)
D <- as.matrix(dist(xyz))
round(D,2)

residue1     0.00     3.80     7.60     8.50     5.37     3.80
residue2     3.80     0.00     3.80     5.37     3.80     5.37
residue3     7.60     3.80     0.00     3.80     5.37     8.50
residue4     8.50     5.37     3.80     0.00     3.80     7.60
residue5     5.37     3.80     5.37     3.80     0.00     3.80
residue6     3.80     5.37     8.50     7.60     3.80     0.00

The folded-back hypothetical geometry places some non-neighbour positions near each other.

title: Protein structure and structural bioinformatics
text:
2. Define a contact rule
A distance below five angstroms is a teaching cutoff. Exclude immediate sequence neighbours and diagonal entries.


Show R code
contact <- D<5 & abs(row(D)-col(D))>1
pairs <- which(contact & upper.tri(contact),arr.ind=TRUE)
data.frame(residue1=rownames(D)[pairs[,1]],residue2=colnames(D)[pairs[,2]],
 distance_A=D[pairs])


  residue1 residue2 distance_A
1 residue2 residue5        3.8
2 residue1 residue6        3.8


Show R code

image(1:6,1:6,contact,xlab="Residue index",ylab="Residue index",
 col=c("white","#1b9e77"),main="Supplied geometric contact rule")









Contacts describe geometry under the chosen threshold. They are not measured interactions or binding energies.

title: Protein structure and structural bioinformatics
text:
3. Assess threshold dependence
Count contacts at several cutoffs using the same non-neighbour rule.


Show R code
cutoffs <- c(4,5,8)
data.frame(cutoff_A=cutoffs,contacts=vapply(cutoffs,function(cut)
 sum((D<cut & abs(row(D)-col(D))>1)[upper.tri(D)]),integer(1)))


  cutoff_A contacts
1        4        2
2        5        2
3        8        8


A contact list changes when its operational definition changes.

Interpretation and limits
For an actual structure, record accession, model, chain, residue numbering, units, experimental/predicted status and structural uncertainty. A C-alpha cutoff is an abstraction; side chains, ligands, solvent and conformational dynamics affect biological interpretation.

What changes when coordinates are converted to nanometres?
Why exclude sequential neighbours?
Does a contact establish functional necessity?

Values divide by ten and the cutoff must also divide by ten.
They reflect backbone proximity and can obscure non-local geometry.
No; perturbation and functional evidence are needed.

title: RNA-seq counts, contrasts and uncertainty
text:
Biological question and data
Does expression differ between the two diets in a hypothetical 48-animal experiment?
The fixture simulates negative-binomial counts for 24 genes, with independent animals, crossed diet/batch and known multiplicative exposure. The first four genes have a supplied diet effect. Gene01 also has a genotype effect. A quasi-Poisson fit below is an intentionally restricted mean-model illustration; its single variance multiplier per gene is not the generating negative-binomial variance function.
No biological download is required. Numerical inputs are hypothetical, not observed animal data. The runnable examples use base R. Count and abundance units are specified where used.

title: RNA-seq counts, contrasts and uncertainty
section: 3. Fit the mean model and report uncertainty
text:
3. Fit the mean model and report uncertainty
Fit each gene with diet, batch and a log-exposure offset. The diet coefficient uses the natural-log link; divide it and its standard error by log(2) to obtain log2 units.


Show R code
fit_gene <- function(y) {
 fit <- glm(y~diet+batch+offset(log(exposure)),data=meta,family=quasipoisson())
 tab <- coef(summary(fit))
 c(log2_effect=tab["dietsupplement","Estimate"]/log(2),
 SE_log2=tab["dietsupplement","Std. Error"]/log(2),
 p_value=tab["dietsupplement","Pr(>|t|)"],
 variance_multiplier=summary(fit)$dispersion)
}
result <- as.data.frame(t(apply(counts,1,fit_gene)))
result$BH <- p.adjust(result$p_value,"BH")
result$lower <- result$log2_effect-qt(.975,nrow(meta)-3)*result$SE_log2
result$upper <- result$log2_effect+qt(.975,nrow(meta)-3)*result$SE_log2

title: RNA-seq counts, contrasts and uncertainty
text:
Interpretation and limits
This practical teaches design, exposure, contrasts and uncertainty; it is not a production differential-expression pipeline. The DESeq2 workflow adds composition-aware normalization and a gene-level negative-binomial dispersion framework. Gene filtering, relatedness, batch design and larger-scale validation need explicit decisions for real data.

title: RNA-seq counts, contrasts and uncertainty
text:
Exercises

What supplied log2 effect corresponds to .65 on the natural-log scale?
Why is Poisson variance too restrictive for these generated counts?
Change the seed and explain why estimates and adjusted p-values change.
What would a complete treatment–batch confounding problem prevent?







Suggested answers






.65/log(2), about .94; a finite-sample estimate need not equal it.
The generating variance is mu + mu squared/12, greater than mu.
Sampling realization changes, while the generating parameters remain the same.
Separate estimation of diet and batch effects.

title: Functional annotation and pathway enrichment
text:
Biological question and data
Is a selected gene list enriched for a supplied pathway under an explicitly defined selection null?
The gene/pathway table is fictional. Every background gene is eligible, and the null treats a fixed-size selected set as uniformly drawn from that background. Selected genes are supplied for teaching, not discovered by a calibrated genome-wide analysis.
No biological download is required. Numerical inputs are hypothetical, not observed animal data. The runnable examples use base R. Count and abundance units are specified where used.

title: Functional annotation and pathway enrichment
text:
1. Define the eligible universe
Use the 24 assayed gene IDs and a prespecified six-gene list.


Show R code
source("../R/teaching_data.R")
d <- teaching_data()
background <- rownames(d$counts)
selected <- sprintf("gene%02d",1:6)
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(background),all(selected%in%background))
annotation <- d$annotation
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(annotation$gene),setequal(annotation$gene,background))
table(annotation$pathway)



pathwayA pathwayB pathwayC 
       8        8        8 


The measured universe is known. Counting annotations outside it would change the null population.

title: Functional annotation and pathway enrichment
text:
2. Calculate enrichment
For each set, compute overlap, null expectation and an upper-tail hypergeometric p-value. Confirm the first result with a 2-by-2 Fisher test.


Show R code
one_set <- function(pathway) {
 member <- annotation$gene[annotation$pathway==pathway]
 N <- length(background); K <- length(member); n <- length(selected)
 x <- sum(selected%in%member)
 c(N=N,K=K,n=n,x=x,expected=n*K/N,p=phyper(x-1,K,N-K,n,lower.tail=FALSE))
}
result <- as.data.frame(t(vapply(unique(annotation$pathway),one_set,numeric(6))))
result$BH <- p.adjust(result$p,"BH")
result


          N K n x expected          p           BH
pathwayA 24 8 6 6        2 0.00020803 0.0006240899
pathwayB 24 8 6 0        2 1.00000000 1.0000000000
pathwayC 24 8 6 0        2 1.00000000 1.0000000000


Show R code
z <- result[1,]
tab <- matrix(c(z$x,z$n-z$x,z$K-z$x,z$N-z$K-z$n+z$x),2,byrow=TRUE)
stopifnot(abs(fisher.test(tab,alternative="greater")$p.value-z$p)<1e-12)


PathwayA has six selected members in a background of eight pathway members. The enrichment model concerns gene-set representation, not measured pathway activity.

title: Functional annotation and pathway enrichment
section: 3. Change the background and explain the effect
text:
3. Change the background and explain the effect
Keep the pathway count fixed while adding unmeasured nonmembers to the universe. This is deliberately an inappropriate comparison for the same assay.


Show R code
data.frame(background=c("eligible panel","inflated universe"),
 N=c(24,100),p=c(phyper(5,8,16,6,lower.tail=FALSE),
 phyper(5,8,92,6,lower.tail=FALSE)))


         background   N           p
1    eligible panel  24 2.08030e-04
2 inflated universe 100 2.34889e-08


Adding many nonmembers makes the same overlap appear more surprising. That is a change in assumptions, not more biological evidence.

title: Functional annotation and pathway enrichment
text:
Interpretation and limits
Hypergeometric enrichment assumes an appropriate equal-selection null. Expression level, feature length, detectability, correlation and annotation overlap can require a more suitable method. Document mapping, set version, selection rule, background and multiplicity.

Exercises

Why exclude unmeasured genes from this universe?
Does a small p-value establish pathway activation?
What if one measured gene maps to three proteins?







Suggested answers






They could not have entered the selected list under this assay.
No; it is evidence about representation under the supplied null.
Define the gene/protein analysis unit and avoid counting repeated gene evidence as independent entries.

title: Biological network construction and interpretation
text:
Biological question and data
Which hypothetical proteins show correlated abundance across the same animals?
The complete log2 protein table contains a supplied shared latent factor and independent noise. A correlation network is descriptive. Animal observations are paired across proteins, and edges are not directional or causal.
No biological download is required. Numerical inputs are hypothetical, not observed animal data. The runnable examples use base R. Count and abundance units are specified where used.

title: Biological network construction and interpretation
text:
2. Define edges and calculate degree
Use a supplied absolute-correlation cutoff of .55. Remove self-edges and count each undirected edge once.


Show R code
cutoff <- .55
A <- abs(C)>=cutoff; diag(A) <- FALSE
edges <- which(A & upper.tri(A),arr.ind=TRUE)
degree <- rowSums(A)
data.frame(protein=colnames(X),degree)

}
points(pos,pch=19,col="#1b9e77",cex=1.5)
text(pos,labels=colnames(X),pos=3,cex=.7)

text:
3. Examine threshold dependence
Use the same variables and animals for each threshold.


Show R code
threshold <- c(.3,.55,.75)
data.frame(threshold,edges=vapply(threshold,function(t)
 sum((abs(C)>=t)[upper.tri(C)]),integer(1)))

2      0.55    16
3      0.75     3


Connectivity changes with the chosen threshold; a hub designation should state that dependence.

title: Biological network construction and interpretation
text:
Interpretation and limits
Correlation can reflect diet, genotype, tissue mixture, batch or other common drivers. A network inferred from abundance is not equivalent to a curated interaction database. The threshold is supplied rather than selected to optimize a biological story; stability is assessed in the biomarker practical.

title: Biological network construction and interpretation
text:
Exercises

Why is the diagonal removed?
Could a batch shift create an apparent module?
Why is the sum of degrees twice the edge count?







Suggested answers






A feature’s self-correlation is not an inter-feature relationship.
Yes; shared technical variation can correlate many measurements.
Each undirected edge contributes one degree to each endpoint.

title: Biological data visualization with explicit units
text:
Biological question and data
Which plots reveal library-panel size, sample variation and possible confounding in a hypothetical experiment?
The shared fixture contains counts, log2 abundances and a response in arbitrary units. The plotted count-panel total includes only the 24 supplied features and is not a whole-library sequencing-depth estimate.
No biological download is required. Numerical inputs are hypothetical, not observed animal data. The runnable examples use base R. Count and abundance units are specified where used.

1. Inspect the design before the measurements
Count independent animals within the crossed diet/batch design.

2. Compare count and abundance views
Use exposure-adjusted counts on a descriptive log2 scale for one gene, and already-log2 measurements for a protein.

par(mfrow=c(1,2))
boxplot(log2(normalized[1,]+1)~meta$diet,xlab="Diet",ylab="log2 adjusted count + 1",
 main="gene01",col="#86B7A3")
boxplot(d$protein[1,]~meta$diet,xlab="Diet",ylab="Supplied log2 abundance",
 main="protein01",col="#E5A66B")









Show R code
par(mfrow=c(1,1))

section: 3. Show outcome distributions and paired measurements
text:
3. Show outcome distributions and paired measurements
Keep animal alignment explicit and label the outcome units.


Show R code

plot(d$protein[1,],meta$response,col=as.integer(meta$diet),pch=19,

title: Biological data visualization with explicit units

Interpretation and limits
Plots diagnose patterns; they do not replace a model or prove an effect. Avoid using different transformations without labelling them, selectively hiding outliers or interpreting one unusual point before checking its identity and processing.

Exercises

Why label the response as arbitrary units?
What could a pooled scatterplot hide?
Why is a plot of log2 counts not a differential-expression test?







Suggested answers






The fixture defines no physical calibration for the phenotype.
Different relationships within groups, batch shifts or unequal sampling.
It supplies neither the required model-based uncertainty nor multiplicity treatment.

title: Scientific reporting and reproducible analysis records
text:
Biological question and data
What evidence and processing record should accompany a computational result?
The example fits a simple animal-level response model to fictional data. Diet allocation, independence and the chosen covariates are assumptions of this teaching design. The report records a conditional estimate, not a livestock recommendation.
No biological download is required. Numerical inputs are hypothetical, not observed animal data. The runnable examples use base R. Count and abundance units are specified where used.

1. Define and fit the analysis

meta <- d$metadata;meta$dosage <- d$genotypes[meta$animal,"marker1"]
fit <- lm(response~diet+batch+dosage,data=meta)

title: Scientific reporting and reproducible analysis records
section: 3. Write the interpretation at the level supported
text:
3. Write the interpretation at the level supported
Separate result, limitation and follow-up. The generated sentence deliberately avoids a causal-mechanism claim.


Show R code
cat(sprintf("Among %d fictional animals, the adjusted diet contrast is %.2f arbitrary units (95%% model interval %.2f to %.2f).\n",

Among 48 fictional animals, the adjusted diet contrast is 1.92 arbitrary units (95% model interval 1.30 to 2.53).

title: Scientific reporting and reproducible analysis records
text:
Interpretation and limits
A real report needs species/population, measurement units, design, permissions, assay processing, software, missingness, diagnostics, validation and uncertainty. Tables and plots should allow readers to assess the conclusion without relying on an unexplained significant/not-significant label.

Exercises

Name one claim the result cannot support.
What changes if ten animals are excluded after looking at their outcomes?
Which parts of a report remain useful when data cannot be public?







Suggested answers






A specific molecular mechanism or a dependable effect in another farm/population.
Selection may bias the estimate; document and justify exclusions and assess sensitivity.
Methods, variable definitions, provenance, permissions/access process and a non-sensitive reproducible demonstration.

title: Sample identity, table joins and missing assays
text:
Biological question and data
What happens when protein columns arrive in a different order from phenotype metadata?
Every fixture animal has an assay identifier. The shuffled column order is deliberate; the underlying biological labels remain correct. This checks metadata alignment, not physical sample identity.
No biological download is required. Numerical inputs are hypothetical, not observed animal data. The runnable examples use base R. Count and abundance units are specified where used.

title: Sample identity, table joins and missing assays
text:
1. Create a plausible order mismatch
Reverse the assay order while leaving labels attached. Dimensions still match.


Show R code
source("../R/teaching_data.R")
d <- teaching_data()
meta <- d$metadata
shuffled <- d$protein[,rev(seq_len(ncol(d$protein))),drop=FALSE]
stopifnot(ncol(shuffled)==nrow(meta),!identical(colnames(shuffled),meta$animal))
head(data.frame(metadata_animal=meta$animal,assay_column=colnames(shuffled)))


  metadata_animal assay_column
1        animal01     animal48
2        animal02     animal47
3        animal03     animal46
4        animal04     animal45
5        animal05     animal44
6        animal06     animal43


A dimension check alone cannot identify this mistake.

title: Sample identity, table joins and missing assays
text:
2. Align explicitly and verify identity
Require unique IDs and complete matches before reordering.


Show R code
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(meta$animal),!anyDuplicated(colnames(shuffled)))
idx <- match(meta$animal,colnames(shuffled))
stopifnot(!anyNA(idx))
aligned <- shuffled[,idx,drop=FALSE]
stopifnot(identical(colnames(aligned),meta$animal),
 max(abs(aligned-d$protein))<1e-12)
c(correct_cor=cor(aligned[1,],meta$response),
 wrong_order_cor=cor(shuffled[1,],meta$response))


    correct_cor wrong_order_cor 
      0.1567479      -0.1811823 


The correctly aligned table reproduces the original measurements exactly. A wrong-order association can disappear or change direction.

title: Sample identity, table joins and missing assays
section: 3. Separate missing animals from missing features
text:
3. Separate missing animals from missing features
Remove one entire assay column and compare this to NAs within otherwise present assays.


Show R code
partial <- aligned[,-1,drop=FALSE]
index <- match(meta$animal,colnames(partial))
c(animals_without_assay=sum(is.na(index)),
 missing_feature_values=sum(is.na(d$protein_missing)))


 animals_without_assay missing_feature_values 
                     1                     11 


Show R code

An absent assay and an unobserved protein value need different handling and reporting. Neither is a measured zero.

title: Sample identity, table joins and missing assays
text:
Interpretation and limits
ID matching preserves supplied labels but cannot detect a mislabeled specimen collected in the field. Use collection records and appropriate sample-identity checks for real data. Avoid silent complete-case deletion when missing assays relate to treatment or health.

title: Sample identity, table joins and missing assays
text:
Exercises

Why does a sorted join still need an identity check?
What if one metadata animal has two assay columns?
Why is a missing protein value not log2 zero?







Suggested answers






Sorting conventions and keys can differ between tables.
Define technical replicates or repeated specimens explicitly; do not choose a duplicate silently.
Missing means unobserved; log2 zero corresponds to an original-scale value of one.

title: Multi-omics experimental design in animal production
text:
Biological question and data
How should an individually allocated diet study collect molecular profiles and later performance measurements?
The hypothetical design allocates diet to individual animals. Pen-allocated diets would require a different unit and replication plan. The practical specifies metadata and tests design identifiability; it does not establish sample size or a collection protocol for a real assay.
No biological download is required. Numerical inputs are hypothetical, not observed animal data. The runnable examples use base R. Count and abundance units are specified where used.

1. Build a matched sample sheet
Keep animal, diet and batch separate from the assay-specific specimen identifiers.

 diet=factor(rep(c("control","supplement"),6)),
 batch=factor(rep(c("A","A","B","B"),3)),
 tissue="liver",collection_day=14)

title: Multi-omics experimental design in animal production
text:
2. Check estimability
Contrast a crossed design with perfect treatment–batch confounding.


Show R code
X <- model.matrix(~diet+batch,plan)
bad <- plan;bad$batch <- bad$diet
Xbad <- model.matrix(~diet+batch,bad)
rbind(crossed=c(columns=ncol(X),rank=qr(X)$rank),
 confounded=c(columns=ncol(Xbad),rank=qr(Xbad)$rank))


           columns rank
crossed          3    3
confounded       3    2


Show R code

title: Multi-omics experimental design in animal production
text:
3. Plan decision timing and missingness
Specify the predictor window and outcome window before inspecting results.


Show R code
decisions <- data.frame(item=c("genotype","day14 assays","future performance"),
 available_day=c(0,14,28),role=c("baseline covariate","candidate day14 predictor","outcome"))
decisions


                item available_day                      role
1           genotype             0        baseline covariate
2       day14 assays            14 candidate day14 predictor
3 future performance            28                   outcome


Show R code

The future outcome can evaluate a day14 prediction; it cannot be included as input to that prediction. Predefine how absent assays and failed QC affect the analysis population.

title: Multi-omics experimental design in animal production
text:
Interpretation and limits
Randomization and blocking, tissue/time, sex, farm, batch, handling and exclusion rules need a justified study-specific plan. Technical aliquots are not independent animals. Use NC3Rs design guidance for the design principles; the invented sheet is not a laboratory sampling instruction.

If diet is assigned to pens, what changes?
Why can adding animals within the same confounded batches fail to solve the problem?
What must be decided before selecting an integration method?







Suggested answers






Pen-level allocation and dependence become central; sufficient independent pens are needed.
The treatment and batch columns remain dependent.
Question, samples, matching, time, measurement scales, missingness, covariates and validation target.

title: Quality assessment and preprocessing across omics layers
text:
Biological question and data
Can the same quality rule and transformation be applied indiscriminately to counts, protein abundances and metabolites?
Counts are nonnegative integer measurements; protein and metabolite matrices are supplied log2 abundances. Missing proteins are deliberately inserted. All samples are fictional animals with explicit metadata.
No biological download is required. Numerical inputs are hypothetical, not observed animal data. The runnable examples use base R. Count and abundance units are specified where used.

title: Quality assessment and preprocessing across omics layers
text:
1. Audit each assay separately
Check IDs, dimensions, missingness and the supplied measurement scale.


Show R code
source("../R/teaching_data.R")
d <- teaching_data()
assays <- list(counts=d$counts,protein=d$protein_missing,metabolite=d$metabolite)
audit <- do.call(rbind,lapply(names(assays),function(name) {
 X <- assays[[name]]
 stopifnot(identical(colnames(X),d$metadata$animal))
 data.frame(assay=name,features=nrow(X),animals=ncol(X),missing=sum(is.na(X)),
 observed_min=min(X,na.rm=TRUE),observed_max=max(X,na.rm=TRUE))
}))

2    protein        8      48      11     6.248562    12.117980
3 metabolite        6      48       0     2.356815     9.467836


The missingness total is not interchangeable with a count of missing animals. Different assays have different physical and statistical meanings.

title: Quality assessment and preprocessing across omics layers
section: 3. Define a stated feature policy and transform correctly
text:
3. Define a stated feature policy and transform correctly
The example retains features with no missing measurements for descriptive PCA. The threshold is a teaching choice.


Show R code
keep <- missing_feature==0
complete <- P[keep,,drop=FALSE]
count_log <- log2(sweep(d$counts,2,d$exposure,"/")+1)
c(retained_proteins=nrow(complete),removed_proteins=sum(!keep))


retained_proteins  removed_proteins 
                6                 2 


Show R code

Protein values are already log2; logging them again would change their interpretation. The count transformation is descriptive, not a differential-expression model.

title: Quality assessment and preprocessing across omics layers
text:
Interpretation and limits
Complete-feature selection excludes signals with missingness and can change the biological question. Imputation and filtering should be justified and fitted within training splits for prediction. Panel counts are not true total sequencing depth, and an abundance profile cannot replace identification/platform QC.

Exercises

Why is a universal log transformation unsafe?
Is deleting every animal with any NA unbiased?
Which preprocessing decisions must stay within training data?







Suggested answers






Measurements may already be logged, include legitimate zeros, or have different scales.
Not necessarily; excluded animals can differ systematically.
Data-derived filtering, scaling, imputation, feature selection and model tuning.

title: Metabolomics processing, standards and feature interpretation
text:
Biological question and data
How does an internal standard help distinguish instrument drift from a supplied concentration pattern?
The first calculation has an ideal shared drift factor affecting analyte and standard equally. The fixture metabolite table is already log2 arbitrary abundance; its feature labels do not identify actual compounds.
No biological download is required. Numerical inputs are hypothetical, not observed animal data. The runnable examples use base R. Count and abundance units are specified where used.

title: Metabolomics processing, standards and feature interpretation
text:
1. Test an ideal measurement correction
An analyte and a standard are multiplied by the same hypothetical response factor.


Show R code
concentration <- c(2,3,5,4,3,6)
drift <- c(.8,.9,1,1.1,1.2,1.3)
raw <- concentration*drift
standard <- 10*drift
corrected <- 10*raw/standard
data.frame(concentration,raw,standard,corrected)


  concentration raw standard corrected
1             2 1.6        8         2
2             3 2.7        9         3
3             5 5.0       10         5
4             4 4.4       11         4
5             3 3.6       12         3
6             6 7.8       13         6


Show R code
stopifnot(max(abs(corrected-concentration))<1e-12)


Correction is exact only because the generating process supplies a shared multiplier and a stable standard.

title: Metabolomics processing, standards and feature interpretation
text:
2. Break the standard assumption
Allow analyte response to vary differently from the standard.


Show R code
analyte_drift <- drift*c(1,.95,1.1,.9,1.05,1)
biased <- 10*(concentration*analyte_drift)/standard
data.frame(concentration,estimate=biased,error=biased-concentration)


  concentration estimate error
1             2     2.00  0.00
2             3     2.85 -0.15
3             5     5.50  0.50
4             4     3.60 -0.40
5             3     3.15  0.15
6             6     6.00  0.00


A standard cannot correct variation it does not track. Chemical properties and preparation can give different responses.

section: 3. Explore a separate log2 feature panel
text:

Maintain labels and scales before plotting. The annotation-confidence labels are fictional examples.

M <- d$metabolite
identity <- data.frame(feature=rownames(M),assignment=c("hypothetical named candidate","unresolved feature",
 "unresolved feature","hypothetical named candidate","unresolved feature","unresolved feature"))
identity

1 feature01 hypothetical named candidate
2 feature02           unresolved feature
3 feature03           unresolved feature
4 feature04 hypothetical named candidate
5 feature05           unresolved feature
6 feature06           unresolved feature

boxplot(M[1,]~d$metadata$diet,xlab="Diet",ylab="Supplied log2 abundance",col="#86B7A3")









Show R code
c(log2_mean_difference=mean(M[1,d$metadata$diet=="supplement"])-
 mean(M[1,d$metadata$diet=="control"]))


log2_mean_difference

title: Metabolomics processing, standards and feature interpretation
text:
Interpretation and limits
Real workflows need blanks, technical QC, drift and batch assessment, detection/identification confidence and justified normalization. The EMBL-EBI metabolite-identification material explains why chemical assignment is separate from signal detection.

text:
Exercises

Why did the imperfect correction fail?
Would another log transform be appropriate for M?
Can an unresolved feature support a named pathway claim?







Suggested answers






The standard did not share the same response factor as the analyte.
No; M already represents log2 abundance.

title: Proteomics analysis and missing-value sensitivity
text:
Biological question and data
How does treating a missing protein measurement as zero change a group comparison?
The supplied values are fictional log2 protein abundances, not raw peptide spectra. Missingness was inserted into the fixture. The contrast is descriptive and does not implement peptide identification, protein inference or a calibrated differential-abundance pipeline.
No biological download is required. Numerical inputs are hypothetical, not observed animal data. The runnable examples use base R. Count and abundance units are specified where used.

title: Proteomics analysis and missing-value sensitivity
text:
1. Count observed measurements
Calculate group-specific observation counts before group means.


Show R code
source("../R/teaching_data.R")
d <- teaching_data()
P <- d$protein_missing; diet <- d$metadata$diet
y <- P[1,]
observed <- tapply(!is.na(y),diet,sum)
means <- tapply(y,diet,mean,na.rm=TRUE)
data.frame(group=names(means),observed=as.vector(observed),mean_log2=as.vector(means))


       group observed mean_log2
1    control       23  7.042704
2 supplement       22  7.036245


Show R code
stopifnot(sum(observed)==45)


The first protein has three missing values. Reporting group means without observation counts hides the change in comparison population.

title: Proteomics analysis and missing-value sensitivity
text:
2. Translate the contrast correctly
The difference in log2 means corresponds to a ratio of geometric means on the original scale.


Show R code
delta <- unname(means["supplement"]-means["control"])
c(log2_difference=delta,geometric_mean_ratio=2^delta)


     log2_difference geometric_mean_ratio 
         -0.00645844           0.99553336 


Show R code
original <- 2^y
geo <- tapply(original,diet,function(z) exp(mean(log(z),na.rm=TRUE)))
stopifnot(abs(geo["supplement"]/geo["control"]-2^delta)<1e-10)


This is not the ratio of arithmetic mean abundance. The calculation concerns the observed values only.

title: Proteomics analysis and missing-value sensitivity
text:
3. Demonstrate an unjustified replacement
Replace NA by zero solely to expose the consequence, then compare the group differences.


Show R code
bad <- y;bad[is.na(bad)] <- 0
bad_means <- tapply(bad,diet,mean)
c(observed_value_difference=delta,
 zero_imputed_difference=unname(bad_means["supplement"]-bad_means["control"]))


observed_value_difference   zero_imputed_difference 
              -0.00645844               -0.29936623 


Show R code
boxplot(y~diet,xlab="Diet",ylab="Observed log2 abundance",col="#E5A66B")









Zero on the log2 scale means original-scale abundance one. It does not represent a valid generic non-observation rule.

title: Proteomics analysis and missing-value sensitivity
text:
Interpretation and limits
Different missing mechanisms require different strategies and sensitivity analyses. Selected complete observations may be biased if detection depends on abundance. Batch adjustment, identification uncertainty, multiple testing and validation are needed for real protein analyses.

title: Proteomics analysis and missing-value sensitivity
text:
Exercises

Why does replacing NA by zero change the contrast?
What if one group has no observed values?
Does a geometric-mean ratio imply a causal diet effect?







Suggested answers






It introduces low observed values where the assay supplied none, potentially unequally across groups.
The observed comparison is not estimable; report this instead of inventing a mean.
No; design, confounding, model uncertainty and sampling determine causal interpretation.

title: Exploratory multi-omics analysis and principal components
text:
Biological question and data
Which sample patterns appear in the hypothetical protein and metabolite panels?
Animals are rows in the PCA inputs; molecular features are columns. Both panels are supplied log2 values and contain shared latent variation by construction. Standardization is used for description, not prediction.
No biological download is required. Numerical inputs are hypothetical, not observed animal data. The runnable examples use base R. Count and abundance units are specified where used.

title: Exploratory multi-omics analysis and principal components
text:
1. Prepare matched feature matrices
Use complete measurements and explicit animal alignment.


Show R code
source("../R/teaching_data.R")
d <- teaching_data()
P <- t(d$protein);M <- t(d$metabolite)
stopifnot(identical(rownames(P),rownames(M)))
X <- cbind(P,M)
fit <- prcomp(X,center=TRUE,scale.=TRUE)
variance_fraction <- fit$sdev^2/sum(fit$sdev^2)
head(variance_fraction)


[1] 0.57849510 0.07719019 0.06658498 0.05267852 0.04811067 0.03908211


Show R code
stopifnot(abs(sum(variance_fraction)-1)<1e-12)


Unit-variance scaling makes different feature variances comparable for this representation. It also gives a noisy low-variance feature greater relative weight.

title: Exploratory multi-omics analysis and principal components
text:
2. Plot scores with design labels
The same PCA scores can be labelled by diet, batch or farm to investigate alternative explanations.


Show R code
plot(fit$x[,1],fit$x[,2],pch=19,col=as.integer(d$metadata$diet),
 xlab="PC1 score",ylab="PC2 score",main="Standardized descriptive PCA")
legend("topleft",levels(d$metadata$diet),pch=19,col=1:2,bty="n")









Show R code
loadings <- fit$rotation[,1]
head(sort(abs(loadings),decreasing=TRUE))


protein08 protein07 feature06 feature05 protein03 protein06 
0.3224110 0.3203770 0.3060873 0.3017077 0.2920050 0.2894331 


Loadings describe feature contributions to a mathematical direction. A sign can flip without changing the PCA representation.

title: Exploratory multi-omics analysis and principal components
text:
3. Demonstrate unit sensitivity
Multiply one feature by 100 and compare covariance PCA to standardized PCA.


Show R code
changed <- X;changed[,1] <- 100*changed[,1]
raw_pca <- prcomp(changed,center=TRUE,scale.=FALSE)
scaled_pca <- prcomp(changed,center=TRUE,scale.=TRUE)
c(covariance_PC1_fraction=raw_pca$sdev[1]^2/sum(raw_pca$sdev^2),
 standardized_PC1_fraction=scaled_pca$sdev[1]^2/sum(scaled_pca$sdev^2))


  covariance_PC1_fraction standardized_PC1_fraction 
                0.9961177                 0.5784951 


Show R code
stopifnot(max(abs(abs(cor(fit$x[,1],scaled_pca$x[,1]))-1))<1e-10)


Positive unit rescaling is cancelled by standardization, while covariance PCA can become dominated by the rescaled feature.

title: Exploratory multi-omics analysis and principal components
text:
Interpretation and limits
PCA is an exploratory linear representation, not an independent test of treatment or a causal network. For prediction, fit scaling and PCA on training animals and project test animals using those parameters. Select the interpretation after considering batch, biological covariates and sampling.

Exercises

Why can a loading sign reverse?
Does a visible diet cluster prove the intervention mechanism?
Why is fitting PCA on train and test together inappropriate for an untouched prediction test?







Suggested answers






An eigenvector and its negative represent the same axis.
No; design and other shared drivers must be examined.
The representation incorporates information from the evaluation population.

title: Regularized regression and held-out prediction
text:
Biological question and data
Do the hypothetical molecular measurements improve prediction for a held-out group of animals?
The response uses arbitrary units and depends on a shared latent factor by construction. Animals 1–32 train the model and 33–48 form a supplied holdout. This split also changes farm composition; its representativeness should be discussed. Lambda is supplied, not chosen using test outcomes.
No biological download is required. Numerical inputs are hypothetical, not observed animal data. The runnable examples use base R. Count and abundance units are specified where used.

title: Regularized regression and held-out prediction
section: 1. Define the split and preprocess using training only
text:
1. Define the split and preprocess using training only
Combine available log2 protein and metabolite features, then estimate their means and scales in training.


Show R code
source("../R/teaching_data.R")
d <- teaching_data()
X <- cbind(t(d$protein),t(d$metabolite));y <- d$metadata$response
train <- 1:32;test <- 33:48
stopifnot(length(intersect(train,test))==0,identical(rownames(X),d$metadata$animal))
center <- colMeans(X[train,,drop=FALSE]);spread <- apply(X[train,,drop=FALSE],2,sd)
stopifnot(all(spread>0))
Z <- scale(X,center,spread)
stopifnot(max(abs(colMeans(Z[train,,drop=FALSE])))<1e-12)
table(d$metadata$farm[train]);table(d$metadata$farm[test])



farm1 farm2 farm3 
   16    16     0 



farm1 farm2 farm3 
    0     0    16 


The test animals do not influence the fitted transformation. The farm composition identifies the transfer task rather than being hidden.

title: Regularized regression and held-out prediction
section: 2. Fit ridge with a separate unpenalized intercept
text:
2. Fit ridge with a separate unpenalized intercept
Use the minimization convention sum of squared errors plus lambda times squared coefficient norm.


Show R code
lambda <- 4
ybar <- mean(y[train])
beta <- solve(crossprod(Z[train,,drop=FALSE])+lambda*diag(ncol(Z)),
 crossprod(Z[train,,drop=FALSE],y[train]-ybar))
pred <- as.vector(ybar+Z[test,,drop=FALSE]%*%beta)
baseline <- rep(ybar,length(test))
normal_equation_error <- max(abs((crossprod(Z[train,,drop=FALSE])+lambda*diag(ncol(Z)))%*%beta-
 crossprod(Z[train,,drop=FALSE],y[train]-ybar)))
stopifnot(normal_equation_error<1e-9)


The penalty shrinks standardized feature coefficients. Its magnitude depends on the stated objective scaling; software conventions can differ.

title: Regularized regression and held-out prediction
section: 3. Evaluate on the same untouched animals
text:
3. Evaluate on the same untouched animals
Compare error and inspect predictions without re-tuning on these scores.


Show R code
rmse <- function(observed,predicted) sqrt(mean((observed-predicted)^2))
data.frame(model=c("training mean","supplied ridge"),
 test_RMSE=c(rmse(y[test],baseline),rmse(y[test],pred)))


           model test_RMSE
1  training mean  1.348718
2 supplied ridge  1.359551


Show R code
plot(pred,y[test],pch=19,xlab="Held-out predicted response",ylab="Observed response (arbitrary units)")
abline(0,1,col="#d95f02")









One split shows the evaluation procedure. The generating model makes useful molecular association plausible, but the test score does not establish practical value in a real livestock population.

title: Regularized regression and held-out prediction
text:
Interpretation and limits
Feature selection, scaling, imputation and lambda tuning must occur inside training-only validation. If lambda is optimized on these test animals, they become a tuning set. For real prediction, use a grouping/time split matching deployment and quantify uncertainty across independent units.

title: Regularized regression and held-out prediction
text:
Exercises

Why is the intercept not penalized here?
What happens if test outcomes select lambda?
Could an accurate predictor be a noncausal proxy?







Suggested answers






The model centers the response separately, leaving the mean outside the coefficient penalty.
The reported score is no longer an untouched test evaluation.
Yes; predictive usefulness does not establish intervention or mediation.
